segments: The Eighth Dynasty.
The Emperors of the Romans.
And he, when he was defeated,
contrived to escape to his own country.
And he went out to Sebastea and again burned it with fire,
because the people were fleeing from before him.
The Romans overtook him,
and he left his pavilion, that is,
his tent and all his baggage,
and fled.
The Romans, moreover, plundered his camp,
and also the fire temple that they were carrying in procession.
Khosrow, then, escaped toward Melitene,
and burned it.
And the Romans again pursued after him;
then the greater part of his army was drowned at the ford of the Euphrates River,
and he escaped with few men.
And he established a law
that a king should not go out to war,
except against a king.
Because the Romans sent to him:
"Since we are the servants of the king,
it is shameful for us to enter and burn like a thief;
how much more so for you, who are a king!" After these things, when the Romans were confident of their victory,
they unsaddled their horses and left them to graze.
And behold, suddenly there came scouts (spies? {OCR?}), that is,
scouts, and said,
"Behold, the Persians are arriving, and Khosrow."
And they were not on their guard at all.
And suddenly the army of the Persians flashed forth,
and panic fell upon the Romans,
and they began fleeing on foot.
And the Persians were pursuing and mocking them,
and they gathered the weapons, armor, and breastplates that the Romans had thrown away and abandoned.
The cause of Justinian's anger against Marcian was this:
There were two factions at that time among the Tayyaye, that is, the Arabs.
Mundhir bar Harith was with the Romans, and he and his forces were Christian,
and Qabus was with the Persians.
And when Qabus came against the Christian Arabs and plundered all their pasture-flocks and herds of their camels, and went away,
Mundhir gathered an army and went against him,
and defeated him, and returned with droves of wealth and camels.
And again Qabus came against him and was defeated,
and he went to the Persians to bring armies.
Mundhir, then, informed the Emperor Justin,
and requested gold from him to give to the forces,
and to stand against the Persians.
Justin, however, plotted to kill Mundhir,
as if on his account the Persians were invading Roman territory.
And he wrote to Marcian while he was encamped against Nisibis:
"Behold, we have written to Mundhir to come to you.
